sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: not located online or in the libraries checked
sources.note: Nothing. Phonology sketch §5.2 (pp. 95-104) covers consonants, vowels, tone (§5.2.2: lexical tone, three levels L/H/Extra-high, tonal sandhi classes), assimilation/elision, phonotactics (CV syllable). Full text searched for stress/accent/prominence/penult etc.: no word-stress statement; 'accent' occurs only as the name of tone diacritics, 'stress' only in non-phonological senses and as 'marked stress and intonational foregrounding' of ideophone performances (general, citing Nuckolls).
Says Siwu is tonal with three level tones and 7 oral/5 nasal vowels; nothing on stress (sources: Dingemanse 2011, Ford 1973, Ford & Iddah 1973).

sources.citation: Dingemanse, Mark. 2017. Expressiveness and system integration: On the typology of ideophones, with special reference to Siwu. STUF – Language Typology and Universals 70(2): 363-385. doi:10.1515/stuf-2017-0018 (MPG PuRe postprint).
sources.note: Nothing on word stress; only tonal change (sandhi) affecting ideophones in bound constructions and 'prosodic foregrounding' of ideophones as performances.

sources.citation: Ameka, Felix K. 2017. The Ghana-Togo Mountain languages: Introduction. STUF - Language Typology and Universals 70(2): 239-244.
sources.note: Six-page issue introduction; only presupposes a 'tonal system' for Lolobi-Siwu, pointing to Ford & Iddah's paper in the same issue; no inventory, no forms, nothing on stress.

tone.quote: Kevin Ford (also a keynote speaker during the 2008 workshop) in collaboration with Robert Iddah, a native speaker of Lolobi-Siwu, presents a thorough description of the tonal system of this variety of Siwu. Indeed the GTM languages have complex tonal systems and their analysis provides discovery procedures for the unlocking of the tonal systems of the other languages.

sources.citation: Agawu, V. Kofi. 1988. Music in the Funeral Traditions of the Akpafu. Ethnomusicology 32(1): 75-105.
sources.note: Ethnomusicology article; asserts Siwu is a tone language (lexical and grammatical tone) on Dakubu 1988's authority, no inventory; Ex. 8a plots one phrase's speech-tone contour on a staff; tones unmarked.

tone.quote: The Akpafu call themselves Mawu ( sing. owu) and their language Siwu or Siwui. ... For our purposes, it is worth bearing in mind that Siwu is not a written language, that a significant degree of bilingualism characterizes the Akpafu area, and that tone (in its lexical, grammatical, and expressive functions) is an important structural feature of the language (Dakubu 1988:137-38).
tone.locator: p. 77, 'Ethnographic background'; cf. p. 75 fn. 1 'Speech tones are, however, not indicated'
